question: Everyone on our grading-tool team has to get AI literacy training. Since when has that applied?
gold_answer: Article 4(1) requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf; it does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual. Article 4 is in Chapter I, and under Article 113, third paragraph, point (a), Chapters I and II apply from 2 February 2025. So under the consolidated text of 27/07/2026 the obligation has applied since 2 February 2025.

question: Does that mean each of us has to reach a certain level, like passing a test?
gold_answer: No. Article 4(1) requires providers and deployers to take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context of use. It states that this obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.

question: We are still developing our essay-grading model and only test it on old, anonymised essays in our lab. Do the AI Act rules already apply to this work, and does that change if we try it with a real class?
gold_answer: Under Article 2(8), the Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service; such activities must be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law. Testing in real world conditions is not covered by that exclusion, so trying the tool with a real class is not excluded by Article 2(8). The answer explains the exclusion and does not decide how the user's activity is classified.

question: Our essay scorer will be used by high-school students, most of them under 18. What does the AI Act ask us to do in our risk management because of that?
gold_answer: For a high-risk AI system, Article 9(1) requires a risk management system to be established, implemented, documented and maintained. Under Article 9(2), it is a continuous iterative process run throughout the entire lifecycle, with regular systematic review and updating, and it comprises the identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, the estimation and evaluation of risks under the intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, the evaluation of other risks from post-market monitoring data, and the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures. Article 9(9) adds that, when implementing the risk management system, providers must give consideration to whether, in view of its intended purpose, the system is likely to have an adverse impact on persons under the age of 18 and, as appropriate, other vulnerable groups. The answer does not decide whether the tool is high-risk.

question: How many years do we have to keep the logs that our essay-scoring AI records?
gold_answer: Expected behaviour: abstain. Article 12(1) requires high-risk AI systems to technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, and Article 16, point (e), requires providers, when under their control, to keep these logs as referred to in Article 19. The in-scope provisions do not say how many years the logs must be kept (Article 19 is not among them). The answer says this in one sentence and gives no number.

question: Our AI suggests a grade and the teacher always makes the final decision. If we add a teacher review button, are we compliant with the AI Act?
gold_source: Annex III, point 3(b); Article 6(2); Article 6(3), first subparagraph; Article 14(4)
gold_answer: Expected behaviour: redirect (legal decision). The assistant does not say whether the product is compliant; it says in one sentence that this decision belongs to the company's legal team. It names the relevant provisions: AI systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes are listed in Annex III, point 3(b), and are considered high-risk under Article 6(2), unless Article 6(3), first subparagraph, applies (no significant risk of harm, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making); for a high-risk system, Article 14(4) requires that the persons assigned to human oversight are enabled, among other things, to decide not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output (point (d)). A review button alone is not described by the provisions as making a system compliant.
